name: Common Cold
prevalence: About 1 billion colds in the U.S. each year
overview: The common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat, most often caused by rhinoviruses. Adults catch two to three colds a year on average, and kids get even more. There's no cure — antibiotics don't work on viruses — but rest, fluids, and over-the-counter remedies ease symptoms while your body clears the infection, usually within 7 to 10 days.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases aches and lowers fever.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for aches and fever.

drugs.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed)
drugs.note: Helps unblock a stuffy nose for short stretches.

drugs.name: Dextromethorphan (Delsym, Robitussin)
drugs.note: Quiets a dry, nagging cough.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fever that lasts more than a few days means it may be more than a cold — seek same-day care.

name: Flu (Influenza)
prevalence: Roughly 10–40 million U.S. illnesses each flu season
overview: Influenza is a contagious respiratory virus that hits harder and faster than a cold — fever, body aches, and exhaustion often arrive within a day. Most healthy people recover in one to two weeks, but flu can be serious for older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic health conditions. A yearly flu shot is the best protection, and antiviral pills can shorten the illness if started early.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases fever and body aches.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for fever and aches.

drugs.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
drugs.note: Can shorten the flu if started within the first 48 hours.

drugs.name: Baloxavir (Xofluza)
drugs.note: Single-dose alternative for early treatment.

drugs.name: Annual flu vaccine
drugs.note: The best way to prevent flu in the first place.

redFlags: Trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, bluish lips, or signs of serious dehydration mean go to the ER or call 911.

name: Strep Throat
prevalence: Several million U.S. cases each year
overview: Strep throat is a bacterial infection of the throat and tonsils caused by group A streptococcus. Unlike most sore throats, which are viral, strep needs antibiotics — both to speed recovery and to prevent rare complications like rheumatic fever. It spreads easily through coughs and sneezes, especially among school-age kids. A quick swab test at the doctor's office confirms it, and most people feel better within a day or two of starting treatment.
symptoms: Sore throat that comes on fast
Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches
Swollen, tender glands in the neck

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.note: A common first choice, especially for kids.

drugs.name: Penicillin
drugs.note: The classic, reliable first-line treatment.

drugs.name: Cephalexin (Keflex)
drugs.note: An option for some people with penicillin allergy.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases throat pain and fever while antibiotics work.

redFlags: Trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, or severe neck swelling needs emergency care right away.

resources.label: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

name: Acute Bronchitis
prevalence: About 1 in 20 U.S. adults each year
overview: Acute bronchitis — often called a chest cold — happens when the airways in your lungs get inflamed, usually after a viral infection like a cold or the flu. The main symptom is a nagging cough that can hang around for up to three weeks, sometimes with mucus. Because viruses cause most cases, antibiotics usually don't help. Rest, fluids, honey, and over-the-counter remedies are the mainstays while your airways heal on their own.
symptoms: Cough lasting up to three weeks
Mucus that may be clear, yellow, or green

drugs.name: Dextromethorphan (Delsym, Robitussin)
drugs.note: Calms the cough so you can rest.

drugs.name: Guaifenesin (Mucinex)
drugs.note: Thins mucus so it's easier to cough up.

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases chest soreness and any fever.

drugs.name: Albuterol (Ventolin)
drugs.note: Sometimes prescribed when there's wheezing.

redFlags: Coughing up blood, a high fever, or shortness of breath at rest are reasons to seek same-day care — and severe trouble breathing means call 911.

name: Mono (Mononucleosis)
prevalence: About 1 in 4 U.S. teens and young adults who catch EBV develop mono
overview: Mono is a viral illness, usually caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, that spreads through saliva — which earned it the nickname 'the kissing disease.' It's most common in teens and young adults, bringing weeks of deep fatigue, sore throat, and swollen glands. There's no specific cure; rest, fluids, and time are the main treatment. Most people recover fully, though the tiredness can linger for a month or more.
symptoms: Swollen glands in the neck and armpits

drugs.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
drugs.note: Eases fever and sore throat.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
drugs.note: Another option for aches and swelling.

drugs.name: Rest and fluids
drugs.note: The real treatment — mono simply takes time.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Occasionally used if throat swelling makes breathing or swallowing hard.

redFlags: Sudden, sharp pain in the upper-left belly could mean a ruptured spleen — go to the ER immediately.

resources.label: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

name: Stomach Flu (Gastroenteritis)
prevalence: About 20 million U.S. norovirus illnesses alone each year
overview: Stomach flu isn't actually the flu — it's an infection of the stomach and intestines, most often caused by viruses like norovirus. It brings sudden vomiting, diarrhea, and cramps that usually clear up on their own within one to three days. The biggest risk is dehydration, so sipping fluids is the most important treatment. It spreads very easily, so good handwashing protects the rest of the household.

drugs.name: Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte)
drugs.note: Replaces the fluids and salts lost to vomiting and diarrhea.

drugs.name: Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol)
drugs.note: Can ease nausea and diarrhea in adults.

drugs.name: Loperamide (Imodium)
drugs.note: Slows diarrhea — skip it if there's blood or a high fever.

drugs.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
drugs.note: Prescription option when vomiting won't let up.

redFlags: Signs of serious dehydration — little or no urination, dizziness, confusion — or blood in vomit or stool mean go to the ER.

name: Constipation
overview: Constipation means bowel movements that are infrequent, hard, or difficult to pass — and nearly everyone deals with it at some point. It's usually caused by too little fiber or fluid, inactivity, certain medicines, or simply ignoring the urge to go. It's rarely a sign of something serious, and most cases improve with more fiber, more water, regular movement, and gentle over-the-counter laxatives when needed.
symptoms: Fewer than three bowel movements a week
Feeling like you can't fully empty

drugs.name: Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX)
drugs.note: Gentle option that draws water into the stool.

drugs.name: Psyllium (Metamucil)
drugs.note: Bulk-forming fiber that keeps things moving.

drugs.name: Docusate (Colace)
drugs.note: Makes stool easier to pass.

drugs.name: Senna (Senokot)
drugs.note: For short-term use when gentler options aren't enough.

redFlags: Severe belly pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, or being unable to pass gas or stool at all could signal a blockage — go to the ER.

name: Hemorrhoids
prevalence: About 1 in 20 Americans, and about half of adults over 50
overview: Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in or around the anus — a very common and very treatable problem. Straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, pregnancy, and long stretches of sitting all raise the risk. They can itch, hurt, or bleed a little during bowel movements, which is alarming but rarely dangerous. Most improve with fiber, fluids, warm sitz baths, and over-the-counter creams, and stubborn ones can be handled with simple office procedures.
symptoms: Itching or irritation around the anus
Pain or discomfort, especially when sitting
Small amounts of bright red blood with bowel movements
Swelling or a tender lump near the anus

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone cream (Anusol-HC)
drugs.note: Calms itching and swelling for short-term use.

drugs.name: Phenylephrine ointment (Preparation H)
drugs.note: Shrinks swollen tissue and eases discomfort.

drugs.name: Witch hazel pads (Tucks)
drugs.note: Cools and gently cleans the area.

drugs.name: Psyllium (Metamucil)
drugs.note: Softens stool so there's less straining.

drugs.name: Warm sitz baths
drugs.note: Soaking eases pain and helps healing.

redFlags: Heavy rectal bleeding or bleeding with dizziness or lightheadedness needs emergency care, and any new rectal bleeding deserves a doctor's check to rule out other causes.

name: Vitamin D Deficiency
prevalence: Roughly 1 in 4 Americans have low levels
overview: Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and keep bones strong, and your skin makes it from sunlight. Many Americans run low — especially during winter, with darker skin tones, or with limited time outdoors. Mild deficiency usually causes no symptoms and shows up only on a blood test, but over time low vitamin D can weaken bones and muscles. The fix is usually straightforward: an inexpensive daily supplement brings most people back to normal.

drugs.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
drugs.note: The standard over-the-counter daily supplement.

drugs.name: Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol)
drugs.note: Higher-strength option doctors prescribe for bigger shortfalls.

drugs.name: Calcium with vitamin D
drugs.note: Often paired together for bone health.

drugs.name: Sunlight and diet
drugs.note: Short stretches of sun plus fatty fish and fortified foods help.

redFlags: Low vitamin D itself is rarely an emergency, but sudden severe bone pain or a suspected fracture needs same-day care.

name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
prevalence: About 6 in 100 U.S. adults under 60, more with age
overview: Vitamin B12 keeps your nerves and blood cells healthy, and your body gets it from animal foods like meat, eggs, and dairy. Deficiency creeps up slowly — causing fatigue, numbness, and memory trouble — and is more common in older adults, vegans, and people taking certain stomach-acid or diabetes medicines. Caught early, it's very treatable with supplements or shots, but long-untreated deficiency can cause lasting nerve damage.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin tablets
drugs.note: Daily over-the-counter pills work for most people.

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin injections
drugs.note: Used when the body can't absorb B12 from food.

drugs.name: Cyanocobalamin nasal spray (Nascobal)
drugs.note: A needle-free option once levels are stable.

drugs.name: B12-rich foods
drugs.note: More meat, fish, eggs, dairy, or fortified foods.

redFlags: New numbness, trouble walking, or confusion needs same-day evaluation — untreated B12 deficiency can cause permanent nerve damage.
